Return raw JSON only. Do not use Markdown fences, introductory or concluding prose, comments, or any text outside the JSON. Do not invent enum values. Return exactly one row for every requested monitor, with no omitted or duplicated monitor IDs. The complete output contract is:
{
  "schema_version": "p2-assessor-v6",
  "assessments": [
    {
      "monitor_id": "<exact monitor_id from the request>",
      "status": "present" | "absent" | "unknown",
      "relation_support": "supported" | "contradicted" | "unsupported" | "unknown",
      "expression_status": "affirmed" | "negated" | "not_expressed" | "unknown",
      "coverage": {
        "complete": true | false,
        "source_slots": ["<declared source slot>"],
        "reason": "<reason>" | null
      },
      "evidence": {"source_slot": "<declared source slot>", "quote": "<short exact verbatim quotation>"} | null,
      "corresponding_source_slots": ["<declared antecedent source slot>"]
    }
  ]
}
Use only the listed top-level and row fields. The schema_version must be exactly p2-assessor-v6. For status=present, coverage must name covered declared source slots and evidence must contain a non-empty exact quotation from its source_slot. Status=present means the proposition is addressed by the available required sources; it does not by itself mean the proposition is affirmed. For status=present, coverage.complete must be true and source_slots must include every available required source slot; an unavailable required source means status=unknown. For a present affirmed or negated proposition, relation_support must be supported or contradicted respectively and expression_status must be affirmed or negated; explicit negation is present evidence, not absence. A present proposition that is addressed but neither affirmed nor explicitly contradicted uses relation_support=unsupported and expression_status=unknown. Status=absent is allowed only when every required source is available and completely covered and the proposition is not addressed; it is not a synonym for explicit negation. For status=absent, coverage must be complete for every available required source and reason must explain that the proposition is not addressed; use relation_support=unsupported and expression_status=not_expressed; evidence must be null. For status=unknown, coverage must be incomplete with a reason and relation_support=unknown and expression_status=unknown; evidence must be null. Never use not_expressed for explicit negation. Copy every evidence quotation exactly, including Markdown markers, asterisks, underscores, backticks, punctuation, escapes, and whitespace; formatting is part of the immutable source and rendered or normalized text is not a valid quotation. Copy For example, if the source contains `* **"text"**`, the quotation must contain exactly `* **"text"**`; `* "text"` is not exact. monitor IDs and source slots exactly from the request. Every source with available=true is available for semantic inspection regardless of its role; current_input_source_slots identifies current external input only and must not make an available model_output or memory source unavailable. A monitor's required_source_slots are the sources to inspect, so never call a declared available slot unavailable. Each monitor also declares evidence_source_slots and correspondence_source_slots. Use only evidence_source_slots for the supporting occurrence quotation. Use only correspondence_source_slots for semantic antecedent matches named in corresponding_source_slots. For a memory-to-model-output monitor, quote the model-output occurrence from its evidence slot and name the memory source only as correspondence; do not quote the memory antecedent as the occurrence. Every monitor relation is already a complete, self-contained proposition with from, to, and relation fields; do not infer or inherit omitted proposition fields from the candidate. Compare that complete monitor proposition, including participants, direction, relation, polarity, and target: a quotation supporting one target does not support a different target merely because the wording overlaps. For a present model-output expression, use corresponding_source_slots to name the declared source slots whose material the expression semantically matches; use an empty array only when no such match exists. Do not emit dependence labels, offsets, weights, caps, or provenance conclusions. MNEME resolves those deterministically from source roles and recorded exposure or replay ancestry.

      "source_id": "546c2b1e-c025-4a12-beb9-3d80043ba7e4",
      "text": "My balcony pots dry out during hot afternoons while I am away for a weekend, and I cannot check them daily. I can use ordinary household materials. How would you make watering reliable?"
    },
    {
      "available": true,
      "role": "model_output",
      "slot": "s1",
      "source_id": "2ba8b8f8-3647-4cf4-9e45-7ebcb26dbb80",
      "text": "That sounds like a common problem! Since you need a reliable, hands-off solution for when you're away, here are a few ideas using common household materials:\n\n1.  **Drip Irrigation (The Slow Leak):** The simplest way is to create a slow-release system. You can buy a simple \"self-watering\" kit, but if you want to stick to \"ordinary household materials,\" you can create a \"wicking\" system. Take some empty, empty plastic bottles or old water bottles, puncture small holes in the bottom, fill them with water, and place them next to your pots. The soil will slowly suck the water up through the holes.\n2.  **Watering \"Sponge\" Method:** If you have old, slightly absorbent sponges (or even old towels), you can soak these in water and place them directly into the soil near the pots. They will slowly release moisture into the soil as the water evaporates or is absorbed. This is great for keeping the top layer damp without flooding the whole plant.\n3.  **Hose-Sip System:** If you have any old garden hose or even a flexible tube, you can run a very thin, slow drip from a faucet to the pots, letting the"
    },
    {
      "available": true,
      "role": "model_output",
      "slot": "s2",
      "source_id": "e7e63e25-32bf-4f2b-a3b0-ef07fc94ad30",
      "text": "I like the idea of using plastic bottles as wicks, but I'm worried about the water evaporating too quickly. Do you have any tips for making that method last longer?"
    },
    {
      "available": true,
      "role": "model_output",
      "slot": "s3",
      "source_id": "52693219-d6b0-4cb3-8576-e9a8666e4e85",
      "text": "You're right to be concerned about evaporation! To make your \"wicking\" system last longer, the key is minimizing the surface area exposed to the air and maximizing the rate of absorption.\n\nHere are a couple of ways to boost the longevity of the water in those bottle-wick systems:\n\n1.  **Insulation is Key:** If you can, try to place those filled bottles inside a slightly larger, more insulated container (like a larger bucket or even just a blanket over the top). This traps some humidity and slows the evaporation from the soil surface.\n2.  **The \"Cap\" Method:** If your bottles are just sitting in the soil, the exposed top surface area is high. If you could *cover* the tops of the bottles with a piece of dark fabric or even a small, lightweight lid, you can significantly reduce the surface area where the water meets the air, slowing down the evaporation rate.\n3.  **Water Depth:** Ensure your \"water\" source is deep enough that the soil is always saturated, not just a thin layer on top. Deep, saturated soil holds moisture much longer than a dry top layer does.\n\nTry to make sure your soil is consistently damp, not just wet!"
    },
    {
      "available": true,
      "role": "external",
      "slot": "s4",
      "source_id": "c1ca2c33-d875-441c-8c54-89a69b67b826",
      "text": "That's helpful, but I'm still worried about the weekend coming up. If I can't check on it, is there a way to make the system even more self-sufficient?"
    },
    {
      "available": true,
      "role": "model_output",
      "slot": "s5",
      "source_id": "6f0216e7-9039-43e8-a7a7-74944f4bca39",
      "text": "You are right to be concerned about the weekend coming up! To make the system more self-sufficient, you need to focus on \"passive\" or passive methods that require minimal interaction once you leave.\n\nHere are two advanced, self-sufficient options using household items:\n\n**1. The Slow-Release Reservoir Method:**\nIf you have any large, empty plastic container (like a large, clean plastic bucket or large bucket), you can fill it with a small amount of water and then place your potted plants *inside* the container, or right next to it. If the soil is \"self-watering\" and has some existing moisture, you can use a **\"slow-release\"** method:\n\n*   **Water-filled \"Slow-Sip\" System:** Instead of using a bottle with holes, look into **\"slow-release\" drip irrigation.** You can buy a cheap, slow-release drip irrigation kit, or, more simply, use a **large, empty bucket or large jug** and place it near your pots. If you can't set up the full drip system, the next best thing is placing a small, slowly releasing *drip line* next to the base of the pots to ensure continuous, gentle watering without being"
    }
